interviewQuestions.question: Why did tokenization move from whole words to subwords?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd frame this around two failures of word-level tokenization: it can't handle words outside a fixed vocabulary (rare words, typos, new terms all collapse to a single `<UNK>` token, losing information), and it scales poorly for morphologically rich languages where every inflection of a word becomes its own vocabulary entry. Subword schemes like BPE or WordPiece learn a vocabulary of frequent character chunks bottom-up from a training corpus, so common words stay intact as single tokens for efficiency, while rare or unseen words decompose into known pieces — "unhappiness" becomes "un" + "happi" + "ness" instead of `<UNK>`. That gives a fixed, bounded vocabulary size (typically 30k–50k tokens) with zero out-of-vocabulary failures — worst case it falls back to individual characters or bytes. That's why every modern Transformer (BERT, GPT, T5) uses a subword tokenizer rather than word-level splitting.

**Testing:** whether you understand the out-of-vocabulary problem and the vocabulary-size trade-off, not just that "subwords are used now".
